deep.reconstruction: There is no mathematics on this page. Folio 24 continues German lecture or study notes on ancient (biblical) history, picking up from the previous page's section 'b. Der jüdische Staat als getrenntes Reich 975–588, a) allgemeine Bemerkungen' (the Jewish state as a divided kingdom, general remarks). The points are numbered: II. Wars between the two kingdoms led to alliances with neighbouring peoples, nearly to their ruin (the word is unclear, probably 'Uneinigkeit', disunity). III. The division affected religion: the kings of Israel set up another sanctuary where Jehovah was worshipped (Sichem/Shechem). IV. Even though religion suffered, it kept many adherents. Every misfortune was read as a punishment of Jehovah, so inspired men, the prophets, arose to tell the nation what to do and what to avoid. V. In this period the idea of the Messiah, older among the Jews, first became really alive. Then a heading: 'A. Geschichte des Reichs Israel 975–722' (history of the kingdom of Israel). Israel comprised 10 tribes, while Judah held the capital (Jerusalem). Israel had 19 kings, the first being Jeroboam. Shechem remained the capital until the 6th king, Omri, after which it became Samaria (continued on the next page). The only numbers are historical dates (975, 722) and counts (10 tribes, 19 kings, 6th king). No computation, derivation or mathematical problem appears. The handwriting and content look like school or lecture notes on history, quite possibly not by Gauss himself (perhaps a family member's or student's notebook bound into the bundle).
errors: No mathematical errors, since there is no mathematics. Historically the dates follow the older conventional chronology used in early-19th-century textbooks (division of the kingdom 975 BC, fall of Samaria 722 BC, fall of Jerusalem 588 BC); modern chronology puts these at about 930, 722/721 and 587/586 BC. The figure of 19 kings of Israel matches the traditional count. The claim that Shechem stayed the capital until Omri simplifies the traditional account, in which Tirzah also served as capital before Omri founded Samaria.
deep.surprise_reason: The page holds only history notes on the divided kingdoms of Israel and Judah, with no mathematical content. It is likely not even Gauss's own work.
transcription_corrections: Line 2: 'Sie wurden nun bald[?] Opfer[?] ihrer Reinheit[?]-heit[?]' more plausibly reads 'Sie wurden nun fast Opfer ihrer Uneinig-keit' ('they nearly became victims of their disunity'). This is uncertain.

Section IV, line 1: 'immer beschützt wurde' is doubtful. The concessive 'Wenn auch ... so war es doch natürlich daß sie viele Anhänger behielt' calls for something like 'vernachlässigt' or 'verletzt' (neglected/violated).
Section IV: the small inserted word above the line (in a different, reddish ink) is uncertain; the reading '{+Schulen+}' is doubtful, and the base text reads 'daß er/sie viele Anhänger behielt'.

Last lines: 'Diesem blieb nur die Hauptstadt bis auf dem 6, König Omri' should read 'Sichem blieb nun die Hauptstadt bis auf den 6. König Omri' ('Shechem remained the capital until the 6th king Omri'). It continues on the next page with '...Jetzt wurde es Samaria'.
Section IV end: 'was sie zu thun[?] und meiden[?] sollten' reads plausibly as 'was sie zu thun und zu meiden hätten/sollten'. The sense is clear.
